<!-- Generated from chromy.Rmd.orig by tools/precompute-vignettes.R; edit the .orig file. -->



Chromy's (1979) method selects units one at a time down an ordered list, each
with probability proportional to its size, so that every unit's realised
number of selections differs from its expected number by less than one —
*probability minimum replacement* — and the sample size is always exact. It
is the procedure behind `PROC SURVEYSELECT METHOD=PPS_SEQ` and behind many
large establishment and household surveys; `chromy` is the method in the
open. This vignette walks through one design from the frame to the estimate.

## A frame

The frame is a data frame with one row per unit. Here, 300 schools in four
regions, with enrolment as the size and an outcome we will estimate.


``` r
library(chromy)
set.seed(2026)

frame <- data.frame(
  region   = sample(c("north", "east", "south", "west"), 300, replace = TRUE),
  district = sample(sprintf("d%02d", 1:20), 300, replace = TRUE),
  pupils   = round(rlnorm(300, meanlog = 4.5, sdlog = 0.9)),
  outcome  = rlnorm(300, meanlog = 5, sdlog = 0.7)
)
head(frame)
#>   region district pupils   outcome
#> 1  north      d02    115 201.00662
#> 2  north      d13     17 192.24854
#> 3  north      d12    585  90.31960
#> 4   east      d07     11  72.72865
#> 5  north      d13    121  47.06255
#> 6  south      d15     73 239.34293
```

## The selection

`chromy_sample()` does the whole procedure: it computes the expected hits
from the size, orders the frame by the sort keys in hierarchical serpentine
order (implicit stratification — the computed size is available to the sort
as `chromy_size`), draws the head of the list with probability proportional
to size, and selects sequentially down the rotated list.


``` r
s <- chromy_sample(
  frame,
  n = 40, size = "pupils",
  order_by = c("region", "district", "chromy_size"),
  seed = 123
)
s
#> <chromy_sample> 40 units, 40 hits, from a frame of 300
#> Head all at list position 218; without replacement.
#> # A tibble: 40 × 12
#>     unit position expected_hits  hits weight fixed_hits random_hits region
#>    <int>    <int>         <dbl> <int>  <dbl>      <dbl>       <dbl> <chr> 
#>  1    34        2        0.313      1   3.19          0           1 south 
#>  2    81        8        0.479      1   2.09          0           1 west  
#>  3   152       17        0.131      1   7.66          0           1 west  
#>  4   228       29        0.0880     1  11.4           0           1 west  
#>  5   149       34        0.854      1   1.17          0           1 west  
#>  6    97       44        0.388      1   2.58          0           1 west  
#>  7   239       50        0.133      1   7.50          0           1 west  
#>  8    69       53        0.222      1   4.50          0           1 west  
#>  9    91       69        0.0340     1  29.4           0           1 west  
#> 10   157       73        0.0586     1  17.1           0           1 west  
#> # ℹ 30 more rows
#> # ℹ 4 more variables: district <chr>, pupils <dbl>, outcome <dbl>,
#> #   chromy_size <dbl>
```

Three properties to notice, none of them approximate:


``` r
sum(s$sample$hits)                       # the sample size is exact
#> [1] 40
sum(s$expected_hits)                     # the expected hits sum to n
#> [1] 40
all(s$sample$hits == floor(s$sample$expected_hits) |
    s$sample$hits == ceiling(s$sample$expected_hits))
#> [1] TRUE
```

The third line is minimum replacement itself: a unit expected 0.3 times is
selected 0 or 1 times, a unit expected 2.4 times is selected 2 or 3 times,
never further from its expectation. Units whose proportional share reaches
one are resolved into certainties (`expected_hits = 1`), so the ordinary
design is without replacement; set `min_replacement = TRUE` to let large
units keep expected hits above one and be selected more than once.

All randomness comes from R's own generator — one `sample.int()` for the
head, one `runif()` per unit — so the `seed` argument (or a prior
`set.seed()`) reproduces the selection exactly.

## The serpentine order

The sort is what makes a sequential selection an implicitly stratified one:
units that sit together in the list are selected apart. A plain nested sort
leaves a seam at every boundary where the largest unit of one group meets
the smallest of the next; the serpentine sort reverses direction at each
boundary, so neighbouring units are always alike.


``` r
toy <- data.frame(
  stratum = rep(c("a", "b"), each = 4),
  size    = c(4, 2, 3, 1, 30, 10, 40, 20)
)
toy[serpentine_order(toy, c("stratum", "size")), ]
#>   stratum size
#> 4       a    1
#> 2       a    2
#> 3       a    3
#> 1       a    4
#> 7       b   40
#> 5       b   30
#> 8       b   20
#> 6       b   10
```

Within stratum `a` the sizes ascend; at the boundary the order turns and
stratum `b` descends — no seam.

## The estimate

`estimate_total()` applies the estimator that matches the design: each
unit's value divided by its *effective* expected hits (the ones the
selection actually used) and weighted by the hits it received, with the
successive-difference variance read in list order over the randomly decided
hits.


``` r
estimate_total(s, "outcome")
#> # A tibble: 1 × 5
#>   variable  total    se cv_pct random_draws
#>   <chr>     <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>        <int>
#> 1 outcome  37623. 5010.   13.3           38
sum(frame$outcome)   # the true total, for comparison
#> [1] 56475.43
```

The sampling weights are on the sample itself, ready for any other
design-based analysis:


``` r
head(s$sample[c("unit", "expected_hits", "hits", "weight")])
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>    unit expected_hits  hits weight
#>   <int>         <dbl> <int>  <dbl>
#> 1    34        0.313      1   3.19
#> 2    81        0.479      1   2.09
#> 3   152        0.131      1   7.66
#> 4   228        0.0880     1  11.4 
#> 5   149        0.854      1   1.17
#> 6    97        0.388      1   2.58
```
